Actually this stuff is specifically designed to allow water to expand in frost conditions without damaging the pavement. Most of the time freeze-thaw damage occurs to concrete due to cracking and water infiltration into the concrete. The large voids in the permeable surface allows water to drain quickly, while any water remaining in the pavement by adhesion has space to expand into.

I suspect it's functionality is entirely dependent on it's substrate material as well. You couldn't, for example, topcoat old or worn concrete and expect it to work like this. You'd need to have a pretty significant excavation to do it right I'd think.

You would be correct. It needs uncompacted soil beneath it to allow the water to exfiltrate. Compacted soil tends to prevent water moving through it as that is a function of a soils ratio of solids and voids. However there are ways to prevent or reduce cracking and allow it to be load bearing and increase the performance of the pavement as a system.

Sinkholes develop from undermining of the underlying substrate like in the situation of underground creeks or rivers (there must be some void which is created below the surface for the ground to collapse into). That tends to happen when water has significant flow rate at an angle which ablates the surface of that substrate (carrying off soil). The pervious surface restricts lateral movement and only allows water to flow directly downward into the subsurface soil below it. That prevents the water from carrying off bits of soil and eliminates undermining. It is, essentially, like a coffee filter.

Gonna get a bit long winded, but it is easier to understand if I describe the whole event than answering simply.

So boot camp itself is nothing more than a way to shape future Marines. I know they are constantly changing the format of boot camp but this is how it was when I went through (August 2nd through October 28th 2005). Boot camp is approx 92 days long broken into receiving, which was a couple days long, and then 3 phases each 4 weeks long. Receiving was nothing more than a shit ton of paperwork, medical checkups, issuing of gear, and some other shit.

Phase one was at Marine Corps Recruit Depot (MCRD) San Diego. This phase is mostly tearing you down as a person plus physical conditioning. You are ran ragged, constantly being yelled at, running all the damn time, and just getting into a routine. When not being fucked with, you were mostly sitting in a classroom called "The Room of Knowledge" learning about a variety of different stuff like Marine Corps history, battle field medicine, military courtesies, and other stuff.

Phase two you get on a bus and are shipped up to Camp Pendleton. Here, the Dis started the rebuilding process as a future Marine. Things get a little less mental and there is a lot more emphasis on the outdoors. During this phase you do all of your basic rifleman classes, plus what we called "snapping in" which is where you literally just practiced the official qualifying stances for shooting which were standing, kneeling, sitting, and prone. You then go onto your range practice and then qualifying at the 200, 300, and 500 yard doing the previously mentioned stances. When I went through it was just with iron sights but I heard that since I got out you are actually able to qual with an ACOG. After range, you go into an outdoors survival section of the training. It covers land navigation, a quick down and dirty on how to survive if you get separated from your brothers, and a lot of hiking.

Phase three you go back to MCRD San Diego and is the light at the end of the tunnel. The DIs calm down a lot, unless you fuck up, and it is more focused on truly turning you into a Marine. The classes become a lot more often, you get some free time to study from your course info, there is one week where you shadow a fleet Marine on base at their job, mine was in a supply warehouse. You finish off, swimming qual, you get tested on your knowledge, you do a written and practical battle medicine, and a couple other things.

During the whole thing, you feel like it is the worst time of your life and you do get a bit down, but looking back, it wasn't as bad as I really thought. I have since forgotten almost everything that I learned in that classroom. Enlisting was one of the best decisions I ever made. Because of the the life skills I learned and the occupation I chose, I am now a 29 year old with zero college credits with a fairly high income. I recommend it to everyone.
